sources.fact: Scientific American, 'Why don't our digestive acids corrode our stomach linings?': the solution in the stomach lumen may have a pH of one or less, about 10 times as acidic as lemon juice; cells in the mucosa secrete large quantities of protective mucus; bicarbonate (HCO3-) trapped in the mucus neutralises HCl that penetrates it

Live Science, 'Why doesn't stomach acid burn through our stomachs?' (Jan 2026): cells produce a thick, sticky, alkaline layer of mucus rich in bicarbonate that protects the stomach lining from its own acid and enzymes

University of Leeds Histology Guide, 'Stomach': surface mucous cells produce a thick coating of mucus that protects the gastric mucosa from acid and enzymes; even so, these cells have to be replaced after 4-6 days

post.instagram_caption:
Your stomach is a bag of acid. So why doesn't it digest itself? 🧪

The fluid inside can reach a pH of 1 or even lower, about 10 times as acidic as lemon juice. The stomach wall protects itself with a thick layer of mucus packed with bicarbonate, which neutralises acid that sneaks in.

Even so, the cells lining your stomach get replaced about every 4 to 6 days.

Sources: Scientific American, Live Science, University of Leeds Histology Guide.
